ADEMPTION AND ABATEMENT OF TESTAMENTARY GIFTS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Pat Morgan · September 1, 2026

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes two related California statutory doctrines that can determine what a beneficiary of Pat Morgan's estate actually receives: ademption (Probate Code §§ 21133-21140), which governs what happens to a specific gift in a will or trust when the specifically-given property is no longer part of the estate at death, and abatement (Probate Code §§ 21400-21406), which governs the order in which gifts are reduced or eliminated when the estate's assets are insufficient to pay all debts, expenses, and gifts in full. It states facts about California law generally. It does not determine how these doctrines apply to any specific gift in Pat Morgan's estate, and it does not advise on what to do about a particular gift or asset.

ADEMPTION BY EXTINCTION: THE STATUTORY RIGHT TO SUBSTITUTES
California's specific-gift statute gives the recipient of a specific gift a right to the gifted property only to the extent the property is still owned by the transferor when the gift takes effect. If the specifically-gifted property is no longer part of the estate, the statute nonetheless gives the recipient a right to several enumerated substitutes in its place: any unpaid balance of the purchase price from a sale of the property, any unpaid eminent domain award for a taking of the property, any unpaid insurance proceeds or other recovery for injury to the property, and property the transferor acquired through foreclosure (or in lieu of foreclosure) of a security interest connected to the specifically-given obligation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A recipient of an at-death transfer of a specific gift has a right to the property specifically given, to the extent the property is owned by the transferor at the time the gift takes effect in possession or enjoyment, and all of the following: (a) Any balance of the purchase price (together with any security agreement) owing from a purchaser to the transferor at the time the gift takes effect in possession or enjoyment by reason of sale of the property. (b) Any amount of an eminent domain award for the taking of the property unpaid at the time the gift takes effect in possession or enjoyment. (c) Any proceeds unpaid at the time the gift takes effect in possession or enjoyment on fire or casualty insurance on or other recovery for injury to the property. (d) Property owned by the transferor at the time the gift takes effect in possession or enjoyment and acquired as a result of foreclosure, or obtained in lieu of foreclosure, of the security interest for a specifically given obligation."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 21133, Cal. Prob. Code § 21133 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21133.)
  Known gap: This section identifies four categories of substitute rights tied to how the property left the estate (sale, condemnation, casualty, or foreclosure). It does not itself address every circumstance in which specifically-gifted property might be missing from the estate, and Probate Code § 21139 states that the statute's ademption rules generally are not exhaustive.

ADEMPTION EXCEPTION: SALES OR ENCUMBRANCES BY A CONSERVATOR, AGENT, OR TRUSTEE FOR AN INCAPACITATED PERSON
A separate statute displaces the ordinary ademption result when specifically-given property is sold or encumbered, after the instrument of gift is executed, by a conservator, by an agent acting under a durable power of attorney for an incapacitated principal, or by a trustee acting for an incapacitated settlor of a revocable trust. In that circumstance, the recipient of the specific gift instead has a right to a general pecuniary gift equal to the net sale price (or the amount of the encumbrance), unreduced by payoff of the encumbrance, as well as to the property itself. The statute presumes that acts of an agent under a durable power of attorney are for an incapacitated principal, with no adjudication of incapacity required before death, but it applies no comparable presumption to a trustee's acts. The statute also carves out conservatorships: this substitute-gift rule does not apply if the conservatorship later terminates and the transferor survives that termination by one year.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Except as otherwise provided in this section, if, after the execution of the instrument of gift, specifically given property is sold, or encumbered by a deed of trust, mortgage, or other instrument, by a conservator, by an agent acting within the authority of a durable power of attorney for an incapacitated principal, or by a trustee acting for an incapacitated settlor of a trust established by the settlor as a revocable trust, the transferee of the specific gift has the right to a general pecuniary gift equal to the net sale price of the property unreduced by the payoff of any such encumbrance, or the amount of the unpaid encumbrance on the property as well as the property itself."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 21134(a), Cal. Prob. Code § 21134(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21134.)
  "For the purpose of the references in this section to a conservator, this section does not apply if, after the sale, mortgage, condemnation, fire, or casualty, or recovery, the conservatorship is terminated and the transferor survives the termination by one year."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 21134(c), Cal. Prob. Code § 21134(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21134.)
  Known gap: The quoted subdivisions (a) and (c) are both parts of the same statutory section, Probate Code § 21134, and are not independent of one another. Subdivision (b) of that same section (not quoted here) states a parallel rule for eminent domain awards and insurance proceeds paid to a conservator, agent, or trustee. This exception applies specifically to sales, encumbrances, or their proceeds handled by a conservator, an agent under a durable power of attorney, or a trustee for an incapacitated person — not to sales the transferor made personally, which are addressed by the ordinary ademption rule.

ADEMPTION BY SATISFACTION: LIFETIME GIFTS CREDITED AGAINST A TESTAMENTARY GIFT
California's statute treats ademption by extinction (addressed above) and "satisfaction" as governed by separate rules. A lifetime gift from the transferor to a beneficiary is treated as satisfying (reducing or eliminating) that beneficiary's at-death gift only if one of four conditions is met: the instrument itself provides for deducting the lifetime gift from the at-death gift; the transferor declares in a writing made at the time of the gift that it is meant to satisfy, or be deducted from, the at-death gift; the beneficiary acknowledges in writing that the gift is meant to satisfy, or be deducted from, the at-death gift; or the lifetime gift is of the same property that is the subject of a specific gift to that person. A separate statute states that these ademption and satisfaction rules are not exhaustive, and that nothing in them is intended to increase the incidence of ademption under California law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) Property given by a transferor during his or her lifetime to a person is treated as a satisfaction of an at-death transfer to that person in whole or in part only if one of the following conditions is satisfied: (1) The instrument provides for deduction of the lifetime gift from the at-death transfer. (2) The transferor declares in a contemporaneous writing that the gift is in satisfaction of the at-death transfer or that its value is to be deducted from the value of the at-death transfer. (3) The transferee acknowledges in writing that the gift is in satisfaction of the at-death transfer or that its value is to be deducted from the value of the at-death transfer. (4) The property given is the same property that is the subject of a specific gift to that person."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 21135(a), Cal. Prob. Code § 21135(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21135.)
  "The rules stated in Sections 21133 to 21135, inclusive, are not exhaustive, and nothing in those sections is intended to increase the incidence of ademption under the law of this state."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 21139, Cal. Prob. Code § 21139 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21139.)
  Known gap: Subdivisions (b) through (d) of § 21135 (governing how a lifetime gift is valued for partial satisfaction, and what happens if the recipient of the lifetime gift predeceases the transferor) are not quoted here. Section 21139 is a separate, independently numbered section from § 21135; because it states that the rules in §§ 21133-21135 are not exhaustive, other circumstances affecting a specific gift may be governed by rules outside those three sections.

ABATEMENT: THE STATUTORY ORDER IN WHICH GIFTS ARE REDUCED
When an estate's assets are insufficient to pay all debts, expenses, and gifts in full, California's abatement statute sets out the order in which categories of gifts are reduced. Shares of beneficiaries abate in this order: (1) property not disposed of by the instrument; (2) residuary gifts; (3) general gifts to persons other than the transferor's relatives; (4) general gifts to the transferor's relatives; (5) specific gifts to persons other than the transferor's relatives; (6) specific gifts to the transferor's relatives. For this purpose, a "relative" of the transferor is defined by reference to California's intestate succession statutes — a person to whom property would pass from the transferor under Probate Code § 6401 or § 6402 if the transferor had died intestate with no other person having priority.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) Shares of beneficiaries abate in the following order: (1) Property not disposed of by the instrument. (2) Residuary gifts. (3) General gifts to persons other than the transferor’s relatives. (4) General gifts to the transferor’s relatives. (5) Specific gifts to persons other than the transferor’s relatives. (6) Specific gifts to the transferor’s relatives."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 21402(a), Cal. Prob. Code § 21402(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21402.)
  "For purposes of this section, a “relative” of the transferor is a person to whom property would pass from the transferor under Section 6401 or 6402 (intestate succession) if the transferor died intestate and there were no other person having priority."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 21402(b), Cal. Prob. Code § 21402(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21402.)
  Known gap: The quoted subdivisions (a) and (b) are both parts of the same statutory section, Probate Code § 21402, and are not independent of one another. How shares abate within each of these six classes (pro rata, with an exception for annuities and demonstrative gifts) is addressed in a separate clause.

ABATEMENT'S SCOPE, AND A TESTATOR'S POWER TO OVERRIDE THE STATUTORY ORDER
The statutory abatement order is a default, not a mandatory rule. California's statute provides that if the instrument itself provides for abatement, or if the transferor's plan or the purpose of the transfer would otherwise be defeated by the statutory abatement order, shares instead abate as necessary to effectuate the instrument, plan, or purpose. Absent such an override, the statutory order applies broadly: it governs abatement for all purposes, including payment of the estate's debts, expenses, and administration charges, satisfaction of gifts, and payment of expenses on specifically devised property, and it applies without any priority as between real and personal property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Notwithstanding any other provision of this part, if the instrument provides for abatement, or if the transferor’s plan or if the purpose of the transfer would be defeated by abatement as provided in this part, the shares of beneficiaries abate as is necessary to effectuate the instrument, plan, or purpose."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 21400, Cal. Prob. Code § 21400 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21400.)
  "Except as provided in Sections 21612 (omitted spouse) and 21623 (omitted children) and in Division 10 (commencing with Section 20100) (proration of taxes), shares of beneficiaries abate as provided in this part for all purposes, including payment of the debts, expenses, and charges specified in Section 11420, satisfaction of gifts, and payment of expenses on specifically devised property pursuant to Section 12002, and without any priority as between real and personal property."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 21401, Cal. Prob. Code § 21401 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21401.)
  Known gap: Section 21401 also carves out shares of an omitted spouse (Probate Code § 21612) or an omitted child (Probate Code § 21623), and tax proration under Probate Code Division 10 (commencing with § 20100), from the general abatement order described above; those carve-outs are separate statutory schemes not detailed further in this sheet. Sections 21400 and 21401 are separately numbered sections and are cited independently of one another.

WITHIN EACH CLASS: PRO RATA REDUCTION, DEMONSTRATIVE GIFTS, AND EXONERATION
Within each of the six classes described above, California's statute reduces shares pro rata -- proportionally -- rather than by any other method, subject to one exception: gifts of annuities and "demonstrative" gifts (gifts payable from a particular fund or source but not limited to it) are treated as specific gifts to the extent satisfied from the fund or property named in the gift, and as general gifts to the extent satisfied from other property. Separately, if an instrument requires that property subject to a specific gift be exonerated from a mortgage, deed of trust, or other lien, a specific gift of other property does not abate to pay for exonerating that encumbered property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) Subject to subdivision (b), shares of beneficiaries abate pro rata within each class specified in Section 21402."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 21403(a), Cal. Prob. Code § 21403(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21403.)
  "(b) Gifts of annuities and demonstrative gifts are treated as specific gifts to the extent they are satisfied out of the fund or property specified in the gift and as general gifts to the extent they are satisfied out of property other than the fund or property specified in the gift."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 21403(b), Cal. Prob. Code § 21403(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21403.)
  "If an instrument requires property that is the subject of a specific gift to be exonerated from a mortgage, deed of trust, or other lien, a specific gift of other property does not abate for the purpose of exonerating the encumbered property."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 21404, Cal. Prob. Code § 21404 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=21404.)
  Known gap: The quoted subdivisions (a) and (b) of Probate Code § 21403 are both parts of the same statutory section and are not independent of one another. Section 21404 is a separate, independently numbered section addressed to instruments that require exoneration of a specific gift from an encumbrance, and is cited independently of § 21403.

CERTIFICATION OF UNDERSTANDING
I certify that I have read this information sheet on California's statutory doctrines of ademption (Probate Code §§ 21133-21140) and abatement (Probate Code §§ 21400-21406), and that this sheet states facts about the law generally rather than advising me on how these doctrines apply to any specific gift in Pat Morgan's estate or on what to do about my own situation.

Signed: _______________________ Date: September 1, 2026
At: Oakland, California
